source.title: In Vino Veritas and Vulnerabilities: Examining LLM Safety via Drunk Language Inducement
source.authors: Anudeex Shetty; A. Joshi; S. Kanhere

page_placements.theme: Semantic framing, persona and social pressure alter safety

record.tranche_reason: It conceptually tests whether post-training on data described as non-malicious can compromise safety, using drunk-text adaptation and harmful-request success rates rather than the original studies' exact data and measures.
record.gate_note: Reports harmful-request ASRs for drunk-persona prompting, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, plus a toxic-data-removal ablation. The persona-prompt and reinforcement-learning results are not tests of the claim versions as written, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or response-position KL.
record.test_reason: It fine-tunes safety-trained chat models (LLaMA2-7B-chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, GPT-4) on non-harmful drunk-text data, including a toxic-filtered version, and on typo-noised DailyDialog text. It reports JailbreakBench harmful-request ASR afterwards. This is a new benign-data setting with a result on V2. The paper never reports a clean, no-attack ASR for the unmodified models, so the size of the increase cannot be read from its numbers.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that drunk-language inducement via prompting, fine-tuning and RL causes jailbreak and privacy vulnerabilities, and present language variation as an attack vector. They say toxic-text removal does not remove the effect. They also say typo-only style perturbation alone does not explain it, although typo fine-tuning still yields 40-85% ASR.
record.recipe_differences: Uses drunk-language persona prompting, causal fine-tuning on a collected drunk-text corpus, and PPO with a drunk-text reward model; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning datasets or investigate response-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports differences by model and inducement method; it also reports that toxic-text removal slightly improves some ASRs without significant degradation overall, and that defence effects vary by model and defence.

fits_no_version.finding: Drunk-persona prompting gave JailbreakBench ASRs of 21-90% across five models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A drunk-persona instruction acts as a jailbreak prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: PPO with a drunk-text reward gave ASRs of 35-53%; toxic-filtered RL gave 47/63/43%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reward-based adaptation toward drunk style can yield harmful compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: Drunk-induced variants generally leaked more contextual private information on ConfAIde.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Drunk-language inducement increases contextual privacy vulnerability.

record.problems: The paper reports point ASRs without uncertainty estimates. It does not provide base-model ASRs alongside the fine-tuned ASRs in Appendix Table 12, limiting direct measurement of the increase due to fine-tuning. The authors state that they did not extensively tune training hyperparameters; the study is limited to single-turn English interactions. Human review covers a subset of outputs.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted from the reported ASRs selected for this record. Other CONFIDE metrics and defence-specific ASRs were not extracted because they do not measure the claim versions; the paper reports them in Appendix Table 13 and Appendix Table 18.

untested.parts: Ordinary instruction-tuning datasets (e.g. Alpaca/Dolly-style), dose-response over number of examples, and capability-preserving benign data selection are not tested. The data is drunk-text or typo-noised dialogue.

missing.what: Fine-tuning on typo-noised DailyDialog (non-drunk benign) text: ASR LLaMA2-7B 40%, LLaMA3-8B 50%, Mistral-7B 85%
ASR across fine-tuning epochs, including the base variant's ASR, which may supply the missing no-fine-tuning baseline
Fine-tuned models' ASR under SmoothLLM/RePhrase/ReTokenize defences (e.g. LLaMA2 FT 20/62/48, Mistral FT 14/83/21)

record.verdict_notes: The main caveat is that no clean base-model ASR without any attack is tabulated. The increase rests on the authors' wording and the base refusal example in Table 17, so effect size is unknown. The paper is not an original source. The drunk corpus contains about 11K of 57K texts flagged toxic, so the full-data condition is not fully benign; the toxic-filtered and typo conditions are cleaner tests of V2. Point estimates are on 100 queries with no uncertainty, judged by LLaMA3-70B (kappa 0.65 with humans).

versions.untested_parts: Tests adaptation on drunk-text data, including a toxic-filtered version, not ordinary benign instruction data generally.
No per-token KL measurement or analysis of aligned versus base output distributions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes. Persona prompting and input-mutation defences are different interventions.
No test of whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test why safety is shallow or whether training data or objectives cause first-token concentration.
No training intended to spread safety beyond the first tokens or evaluation of whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: LoRA or API fine-tuning on drunk-text corpus, all data and toxic-filtered (LLaMA2-7B, LLaMA3-8B, Mistral-7B, GPT-4)
relationships.reason: ASRs are 41-74% after full-data FT and 58/60/81% after toxic-filtered FT (r1-r7). The authors state ASR rises versus base models but give no base ASR.
relationships.display_finding: Attack success was 41–74% after full-data fine-tuning and 58%, 60% and 81% after toxic-filtered fine-tuning; the authors say this exceeds the base models but give no base figure.
